Moth and Gravel, Field Note 12.
The picture stays, an AI

narrated edition of the
published note. We stopped the

local server. The coastline
stayed where it was. So did the

last vessel positions. The
picture still had its shape.

Helsinki above, Tallinn below, a
few marks in the water between

them. There was plenty left to
look at. The connection message

had changed and the age beside
the selected observation kept

growing. That quiet interval
became the useful part of

Coastal Watch. A coastline lends
conviction. Coastal Watch began

with a maritime dashboard in
Rivaries concept defense. A

track plot needed a place to
belong. We gave it a base map,

then worked on selecting a mark
and keeping its record close.

The coastline helped
immediately. A position could be

read in relation to a shore.
Zooming gave the view a

different scale. Selecting a
track linked the mark to a

source, a time, and a short
history. It also made the whole

thing look more settled. A
recognizable coast gives a

drawing some borrowed authority.
The land can be real while every

vessel on it is synthetic. In
this study, that is exactly the

arrangement. Finishing the
picture gave us another

obligation. Make its limits as
easy to find as its details.

There is more than one clock. A
message has an observation time.

The dashboard also has a time
when it received that message.

Those are two useful pieces of
information. A recently received

message can describe an older
position. A connected stream can

carry an aging observation. The
reassuring word connected

answers a question about the
connection. The mark still needs

a time of its own. We kept
observation age and receipt age

separate. The selected record
puts the source and observation

age beside the position and
movement. You can look into one

mark without giving up the
surrounding water. That is a

small arrangement of labels. It
changes what the reader has to

remember. Let the gap become
visible. The server has stopped.

The last position remains. It's
age continues to grow and the

interface offers a reload.
Actual capture from the

synthetic rehearsal. See the
interruption in the short film.

Removing every mark when the
connection drops would remove

useful context too. Leaving the
picture untouched would make the

gap hard to see. In the
prototype, the last position

stays. The connection state
changes. The age continues to

count even though no new message
arrives to prompt it. The

retained position now has a more
modest job. This is where the

last observation put the vessel.
The screen has no new

observation to offer. We made
the interruption by stopping the

local server. The recording
shows that behavior. It does not

tell us whether someone arriving
halfway through the gap would

understand it. Keep the record
within reach. A mark is good at

attracting attention. It's
record gives that attention

somewhere to go. The reported
identifier, source, age, and

recent positions belong
together. A quality figure needs

its own explanation. The
demonstration heuristic in this

dashboard cannot establish a
vessel's identity or intent.

Zooming closer cannot supply
that missing evidence either.

This is where polish becomes
more than a surface. The

selection color needs to connect
the chart and the record. The

words need to say what was
observed. The older position

needs to remain recognizably
older. Ask someone to read the

silence. The next useful study
is quite plain. Show someone the

interrupted view without
explaining it first. Ask where

the selected vessel is, how they
know, and what they would want

to check next. Listen for the
difference between it is here
and it was last seen here.

Then ask them to find the source
and the age. A label can be

present without doing its work.
We have not run that observation

yet. For now, Coastal Watch
gives us a working picture and

the gap we can repeat. Enough to
put a better question in front

of someone. The water stays on
the screen. The account of it
needs to keep its time.

Study scope, working prototype.
What this picture contains. This

note accompanies the Coastal
Watch specimen and its recorded

local rehearsal. The base map
uses natural Earth land

geometry. Vessel tracks are
synthetic. Alert examples are

separate static fixtures. The
dashboard does not run the track

fusion pipeline. The captures
show selection, zoom, and a real

interruption of the local demo
stream. The 27-second silent

film has direct cuts where
capture gaps were removed. The

application source is private.
No operator comprehension result

where operational validation is
established. Inspect the

captures and working record.
Read the source and media

provenance. You have been
listening to Moth and Gravel

Field Notes. The written edition
is at mothandgravel.com.
